I just met with the Los Angeles Fire Department, EPA, and South Coast AQMD for an on-site briefing on the Lineage Logistics fire in Boyle Heights.

Here's what residents need to know:

• Air quality officials report elevated particulate matter from the smoke, which is why masks and other protective measures remain important.
• EPA and AQMD have not reported metals in the air at levels of concern at this time.
• Additional mobile air monitoring units are being deployed to track conditions in neighborhoods surrounding the fire.

While firefighters are making progress, this crisis is not over. The long-term impacts on the community, air quality, and public health will require continued attention and accountability.

My office is staying in close contact with federal, state, and local agencies. If you need assistance or have questions, please reach out to my office and continue following updates from LAFD, EPA, and South Coast AQMD for the latest health and air quality information.

We'll keep fighting to make sure Boyle Heights and East Los Angeles get the resources, transparency, and answers it deserves.

NMED Fails to Investigate Project Ranger Complaints Referred by EPA

The New Mexico Environment Department (NMED) has not investigated Project Ranger complaints that the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Region 6 referred to it, according to NMED's own records. Project Ranger is Castelion Corporation's 1,000-acre hypersonic weapons and rocket-motor testing campus in Sandoval County. It sits over a Calabacillas watershed aquifer recharge zone, about half a mile from Rio Rancho homes.

Residents filed fugitive dust complaints with both NMED and EPA. EPA logged the matter under its Clean Water Act stormwater program and referred the air quality complaints to NMED's Air Quality Enforcement. On October 8th, NMED told EPA its staff would investigate. The day before, NMED staff had written internally that the complaint came from a "habitual reporter" and would be closed "immediately." Public records show no inspection, report or response to EPA since.

An earlier dust complaint, filed June 29th with video of a plume leaving the site, was closed without a site visit. A supervisor directed staff to "[No Further Action, or] NFA, the case and do not begin an investigation."

On October 16th, NMED's enforcement director ordered staff to stop communicating with the complainant, calling Project Ranger "a theoretical project." Two days earlier his staff had written, "This facility is under construction." EPA inspected the site for stormwater compliance on June 11th, and residents are asking why that matter has not been assigned to EPA staff.

The buildings and test stands are finished, yet the facility has no air permit and no formal written determination under state rules. In May 2025, NMED staff found it would be a Major Source of hydrogen chloride (HCl) requiring a federal Title V permit. Ten days later, NMED told the company by email that no permit was needed.

Graffiti removal continued this week in Malibu's Palisades Fire area, with crews removing graffiti from four additional fire-damaged properties on June 24 as part of the City's Graffiti Cleanup Pilot Program.

The voluntary program helps clean up graffiti on private properties within Malibu city limits that were impacted by the Palisades Fire and have graffiti visible from the street. Removing graffiti helps reduce blight, discourage repeat vandalism, improve public safety, and support the community's ongoing recovery and rebuilding efforts.

The City's Code Enforcement Division and Public Works Department began graffiti abatement in late May. To date, 61 eligible properties have been identified, signed consent forms have been received from 29 property owners, 28 additional consent forms are pending, and graffiti has now been removed from 11 properties. Three property owners declined participation.

The program is voluntary and requires property owner permission before work can begin. City staff continue conducting outreach through phone calls, emails, and follow-up communications to encourage participation and answer questions.

The program runs through April 12, 2027. To have graffiti removed from your property through the program, you must provide a signed Trespass Authorization to the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department. To get the process started for your fire-impacted home or business, contact Code Enforcement at or call City Hall at 310-456-2489.

Presidents love to promise things like safer streets and better schools. But the history suggests there's only so much they can do.

Bill Clinton made one of the biggest federal pushes on crime in recent memory. Government auditors later concluded that his effort explained only a sliver of the drop in crime that followed. George W. Bush and Barack Obama both launched ambitious education initiatives, and test scores barely budged.

That isn't necessarily a sign that those presidents screwed up; it's a sign that they didn't have much power in the first place. Most crime is handled by state and local governments. Washington supplies only about a tenth of school funding.

The trouble is that the officials who do hold that power - district attorneys, school board members, city councils - mostly work out of view. Turnout is tiny, the local newspapers that hold them accountable are disappearing, and many of them run for office unopposed. Sometimes that ends in scandal. But it also creates an opportunity for citizens to make a tangible difference in their communities.

Occasionally, stopped at a red light, we see a man approaching our car with a tattered cardboard sign asking for money to buy food. His proximity makes us nervous. As he begins to thank us, the light changes. "Sorry, gotta go." And away we speed. But where did we have to go? Home to dinner? To complain about the city? To ask why somebody has not done something about getting "those people" off the streets? Somebody should. But perhaps that somebody includes us. The Good Samaritan stopped, took responsibility, arranged care, and helped pay for it. Where are today's Good Samaritans? Many already serve in shelters, congregations, recovery programs, and neighborhood organizations. Let us organize that compassion into a partnership with clear responsibilities and measurable results. Government has a shared moral responsibility to help people get off the streets and restore safe public spaces. I would support federal funding for this effort, with strict accountability, but.... Here is how Good Sam would work. First, government would provide matching funds, coordination, and oversight. Participating agencies would help identify housing, coordinate services, establish financial controls, and maintain a public record of spending and results. Second, participating religious institutions would match government financing dollar for dollar by "passing the basket" during services through designated, voluntary Good Sam collections. Every government dollar awarded to a participating institution would require a dollar raised for the program. Participation would be voluntary for institutions and individual donors. Congregations could pool their collections through a shared Good Sam fund, allowing smaller institutions to participate together. Government payments would follow verification of the required private match. This would give congregations a concrete responsibility: help finance the work, help carry it out, and help account for its results. Reports would track dollars spent, verified matching contributions, housing placements, housing retention, and connections to needed care. Independent audits would examine spending. Ineffective providers would face corrective action or replacement, while participants' care continued. The partnership would serve people regardless of faith. Nobody would have to pray, attend worship, or accept religious instruction to receive assistance. Public dollars and matching contributions would support authorized homeless services, with separate accounting from religious activities. FORGING LATINO POWER unearths the roots of Latina/o leaders' lifelong commitments to social service. Their origin stories involve deeply personal, individual experiences that shaped and transformed them. But there are also pivotal shared moments that impacted a generation or entire communities. Lorena Gonzalez, a prominent labor leader and a highly impactful former state legislator, was formed by both.

Lorena's mother was a registered nurse studying at East Los Angeles College (ELAC) when she volunteered to provide medical support on the historic 1964 Mississippi Freedom Summer voter-registration campaign. Impressive as this social-justice commitment may seem to many, in Lorena's family, it was taken as a given, almost as natural as volunteering in local election campaigns, which they did regularly.

Thirty years later, in grad school at Georgetown, Lorena learned of the dramatic battle underway in her home state over the notorious Proposition 187.
